chapter: Basie and life on the road
title: Basie recordings with Sinatra, Sammy Davis and sight reading
summary: His Hello Dollar solo, the Sammy Davis session in Detroit, and sight-reading demands.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: So with the Basie band, I'm looking at the discography again. There's a recording with Basie on June 8th, 1964, but with Frank Sinatra singing.
Yeah. Yeah. I did the thing, Hello Dollar, I did the trumpet solo on that.
Yeah, he recorded, yeah, he did a recording of Hello Dollar.

And a lot of people really thought it was Louis Armstrong until I made a double high C on the end. See, Louis Armstrong, I never heard of him making a double high C. And people said, man, look on Louis Armstrong, as well as he playing, he's going to wait until he get this old and hit a double high C. But it was just me hitting a double high C.
And you also recorded, yeah, that was, you also recorded with Basie and? Frank Sinatra.
And Sammy Davis Jr. Sammy Jr. And Arthur Prysock.
I don't see Arthur Prysock on here. Let me see. With, well, Sammy Davis, and I'm looking at a list of songs as a whole.

Oh, that thing we did with Sammy Davis, man, that was, I'm surprised that record came out all right, see, because Sammy liked to have a lot of people come and follow him around, you know. And we did this thing at 12 o'clock midnight at a theater in Detroit, after everybody left. And he came in there with his entourage and they had whiskey glue. Uh-oh. And they were drinking at some time, and they were sitting down there, and they was talking, and they had to stop the record, making the record to make another tape because somebody hollered out too loud. Quincy wrote the arrangement for the thing, and nobody knew what we were going to rehearse. I mean, we played, because he didn't rehearse. You know, we got there and played all those numbers down, and they put it out. The record was good. Basie just had some good reading musicians in his band. Oh yeah, I'll bet.
He probably always had to do that.

And a lot of time when we go to make a record, we didn't know who wrote the arrangements. We'd just go there and they'd put the arrangements in front of us and we'd just play. I couldn't do that now. Why not? Because I hadn't been reading any music. You got to keep, just like Earl Warren. Earl Warren used to play with basses. He used to play lead alto with the first basses band. He was a terrific reader. But he had been playing with small bands where he didn't have to read, you know, everybody just faking. And Ed Proper, too. So they had a band at the Neese Festival and they had some of the old basses men to come up there and play. And it was really embarrassing the way he played. A lot of people said, man, I thought Buddy could read. I said, he can read. I mean, he could read. Thank you.
